title: Ordinances on Servants, Violence, and Injury
summary: The ordinances that follow the Ten Commandments begin with Hebrew servants, who must go free in the seventh year, and with protections for a daughter sold into service. Then come laws on homicide and refuge, striking or cursing parents, kidnapping, injuries in fights, harm done to slaves, the pregnant woman struck in a brawl, the principle of an eye for an eye, and oxen that gore or fall into open pits.
story: The people asked Moses to hear God's words for them (20:19), and from 21:1 he does. Chapter 20 gave the principles; chapters 21-23 apply them to the ordinary troubles of village life: debt, family, fights, animals, and property. The section is called the Book of the Covenant, after the scroll Moses reads to the people in 24:7. The first case concerns a slave's freedom. A people who have just come out of the house of slavery must now write limits on servitude into their own law, and the seventh-year release echoes the Sabbath rest just commanded in 20:8-11.
historical:
The Book of the Covenant shares form and content with other ancient law collections, above all the Code of Hammurabi, inscribed on a basalt stela around 1750 BC and discovered at Susa in 1901-1902. Both introduce cases with if, and both deal with debt servitude, injuries in quarrels, a pregnant woman struck in a fight, and an ox that gores. Hammurabi limited debt service for a man's family members to three years, where Exodus sets six. The rule for one ox killing another in verse 35 is almost identical to a law in the older Laws of Eshnunna (around 1800 BC), and most scholars conclude that Israel's law drew on a legal tradition shared across the region.

The differences are as telling as the likenesses. In Hammurabi's code penalties vary by class: an eye for an eye applied among the free, but injury to a commoner or a slave was settled in silver. If a builder's house collapsed and killed the owner's son, the builder's son was to be put to death. Exodus has no such punishment of one person for another's crime, it makes the maiming of a slave grounds for freedom (verses 26-27), and it treats the killing of a slave as a crime to be avenged (verse 20). And its law comes as the word of God to a whole people, not the decree of a king.
cultural:
Debt was the usual road into servitude in Israel. A family that lost a harvest might sell a son, a daughter, or itself into service to pay what it owed. The law does not abolish the practice, but it caps it: a Hebrew servant goes free in the seventh year, keeps the wife he brought, and may choose to stay for life, marked by an ear pierced at the household's doorpost. A daughter sold as a servant (verses 7-11) was usually intended as a wife for the master or his son, and the law shields her. If she is rejected she must be redeemed, not sold to outsiders, and if another wife is taken she keeps her food, clothing, and marital rights or goes free.

In a society without police, justice depended on families. When someone was killed, a relative, the avenger of blood, was responsible for pursuing the killer. Verse 13 limits this: an unplanned killing leads to a place of refuge, later the cities of refuge of Numbers 35, while deliberate murder cannot shelter even at God's altar. The death penalty for striking or cursing a parent reflects the household as the foundation of the covenant community; cursing meant repudiating one's parents or calling down harm on them, not a moment of rudeness.
literary: This is case law in its classic form: a heading (verse 1), then cases introduced by if and divided into variations by but. The order moves from persons (servants and dependents) to life (capital crimes in verses 12-17, marked by the refrain must surely be put to death), then to bodily injury and finally to property. The formula in verses 23-25, known by its Latin name lex talionis (the law of retaliation), is a rhythmic list of body parts and wounds. Right after it the principle is applied to slaves in an unexpected way: a master who destroys a slave's eye or tooth loses not his own eye but the slave, who goes free. Verse 22 is debated. The Hebrew says the woman's children come out; many take this as a premature live birth, with the serious injury of verse 23 applying to mother or child, while others take it as a miscarriage, with a fine for the loss of the child and the harsher penalty for harm to the mother. The verse is often cited in modern debates about abortion, and both readings have careful defenders.

outline.t: Release of a Hebrew servant in the seventh year
Protections for a daughter sold as a servant
Crimes punished by death, and a place of refuge
Injuries from fights, to servants, and to a pregnant woman
An ox that gores a person

doctrines.note: These ordinances show the Ten Commandments at work in ordinary disputes. The cases do not cover every situation; they train judges in a way of reasoning that weighs intent, negligence, and proportion, so that the remedy fits the wrong.

Deliberate murder cannot be settled with money, and the law guards people with little power: the debt servant, the daughter sold for debt, the injured worker, the pregnant woman. A master who maims a slave loses him, a limit on ownership that was unusual in its world.

Justice here is proportionate: the penalty must fit the harm and go no further. Intent matters, so an unplanned killing and a planned murder are not treated alike, and negligence that could have been prevented carries real responsibility.

words.note: Mishpat, justice or ordinance. In verse 1 the plural names these laws as rulings for judges to apply. The word covers the whole field of justice: a verdict, a rule, a right, the way things ought to be. Amos would later call for justice to roll on like a river (Amos 5:24); this chapter shows what that meant in the details of village life.

Eved, servant or slave. The same word describes Israel's bondage in Egypt, a king's officials, and Moses as the servant of the LORD. Here it names a Hebrew serving off a debt for up to six years. Translators choose between servant and slave by context; the institution in verses 2-6 is closer to indentured service than to lifelong chattel slavery, though the harsher cases of verses 20-21 remain.

Kopher, ransom: a payment that covers a life. In verse 30 the owner of a known dangerous ox may pay a ransom instead of dying. Numbers 35:31 forbids any ransom for a deliberate murderer, which shows how highly the law valued a murdered life. The same root lies behind the Bible's language of atonement.

christ: Jesus quotes verse 24 in the Sermon on the Mount: “You have heard that it was said, ‘Eye for eye and tooth for tooth.’ But I tell you not to resist an evil person” (Matthew 5:38-39). He does not abolish the rule for courts, where it had always restrained revenge; he refuses to let it govern personal wrongs, calling his followers to absorb injury rather than repay it. The servant who says he loves his master and has his ear pierced (verses 5-6) has sometimes been read as a picture of Christ the willing servant, but that is a devotional application, not the text's intent. Closer to the text is the ransom of verse 30. Jesus says the Son of Man came “to give His life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45), taking up the Old Testament idea that a forfeited life can be redeemed by a price paid in its place.

hard.q: Why does the law regulate slavery instead of forbidding it, and how can verse 21 call a servant property?
hard.a: Verse 21 says a master whose beaten slave survives a day or two is not punished, “since the servant is his property” (literally, his silver). Readers rightly find this hard. Several points are raised in response. The servitude of verses 2-11 is debt service for a fixed term, and Israel's law surrounds it with limits unknown elsewhere: release in the seventh year, freedom for a maimed slave, death for kidnapping (verse 16), and refuge for runaways (Deuteronomy 23:15-16). Verse 20 treats the killing of a slave as a crime to be avenged, and the lesser rule in verse 21 may reflect the difficulty of proving intent when death comes later, with the loss of the slave's work as its own penalty. Many interpreters also point to Jesus' remark that Moses permitted divorce because of hardness of heart (Matthew 19:8), arguing that some laws restrained evils in a fallen society without endorsing them, while the Bible's deeper principles, the image of God, the exodus itself, and the gospel's “neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free” (Galatians 3:28), eventually worked against the institution. Critics reply that these laws were used to defend slavery in later centuries, including in the American South, and that this history has to be faced honestly. Both observations belong in a fair answer.

questions: The first law given to a people just freed from slavery limits slavery among themselves. How should your own experience of being rescued shape how you treat people with less power?
The law separates planned murder from accidental killing. Why does intent matter so much in how we judge wrongdoing, and in how we judge ourselves?
Jesus accepted eye for eye as a limit for courts but refused it as a rule for personal revenge. Where are you most tempted to keep score?
